name: Space Shuttle Enterprise
best_known_for: OV-101 — the prototype orbiter. Renamed from Constitution after a Star Trek fan-letter campaign. Flew the 1977 atmospheric drop-test programme but never reached orbit — converting it to flight-rated proved more expensive than building Challenger from spares
credit: Originally called Constitution, renamed Enterprise after a fan-letter campaign tied to the Star Trek 10th anniversary. Built as a prototype for the Approach and Landing Tests (ALT) — eight captive flights and five free flights from the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft (a modified Boeing 747) over Edwards Air Force Base in 1977. First free flight 1977-08-12 piloted by Fred Haise + Gordon Fullerton — proved the orbiter could glide and land. Did NOT contain propulsion or active TPS tiles; converting Enterprise to a flight-rated vehicle was estimated heavier than building a new orbiter from structural spares, so Challenger was built instead and Enterprise was relegated to ground-test / fit-check duty. Used for vibration testing, launch-pad fit-checks at LC-39, and eventually displayed at the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum's Udvar-Hazy Center 2004-2012, then transferred to the Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum in NYC.

flights.flight_designation: CAPTIVE-INERT 1 (1977-02-18) · first carrying flight on a Boeing 747 SCA; unmanned; no separation
FREE FLIGHT 1 (1977-08-12) · first free flight from the SCA; Haise + Fullerton; first proof Shuttle could glide + land
FREE FLIGHT 2 (1977-09-13) · 2nd free flight; Engle + Truly; pitch-up landing test
FREE FLIGHT 4 (1977-10-12) · 4th free flight; first without tailcone — full orbital aerodynamics
FREE FLIGHT 5 (1977-10-26) · 5th + final free flight; first dry-runway landing; closed the ALT programme
